title: Script and rhetoric
purpose: Lifts the writing technique (point of view, sentence shape, per-item templates, specificity, rhetorical devices) without keeping any of the source's words.
boundary: The swarm lifts technique and structure only. Never store, transcribe or reuse the source's footage, frames, music, voice or script text. Keyframes and spectrograms are temporary analysis files in a scratch directory and are never copied into the format IR or a variant. On-screen text may be quoted only as a locating note in evidence.note, at most 6 words, and narration is never quoted. Patterns replace content words with slots, e.g. 'FACT {n}' or '{number} {unit} {noun}'. Analysing a public video for technique is fine; republishing its content is not.
evidence: captions[] text and timing (caption track or transcription adapter; analysis only, never copied)
inspect: Read the caption text in a scratch file only; count and classify, then delete. Use F1 frames to see on-screen wording roles.
pitfalls: Copying sentences or distinctive phrases into answers
Counting numbers in captions that came from OCR noise
Computing reading level on fewer than 100 words without lowering confidence

methods.measured: A measurement tool produced the value (an evidence.json field or an ffmpeg/ffprobe filter output). Name the tool and the field.
methods.observed: You looked at extracted frames, crops, scopes, spectrograms or waveforms and saw it. Give the timestamps you looked at.
methods.inferred: Reasoned from measured or observed facts, e.g. 'synthetic voice' from flat pitch on a spectrogram. State the reasoning in the note.
methods.assumed: No direct evidence; a default or convention. Use only for gaps the format needs filled, and keep confidence at 0.3 or lower.

pointer_conventions: ir_path is a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) into the Video format IR (contract schema video_re_format_ir).
A final '/-' means 'append this answer to the array' (the RFC 6901 end-of-array token), e.g. /motion/transitions/- or /generation_rules/-.
A '*' segment means 'each array element the answer is about'; the answer must say which elements (for example beats with role 'item'). The lifter resolves '*' to concrete indexes.
Paths under free-form objects (typography.title, typography.captions, typography.labels, audio.narration, audio.music, render_binding.mapping) use the snake_case key named in the question.

answer_types.number: {"value": n, "unit": "..."} optionally with "min" and "max"; becomes an IR observed_number
answer_types.enum: exactly one of the question's choices (a string)
answer_types.text: one technique description, at most 300 characters, no copied content
answer_types.pattern: a template with {slots} in place of content words, e.g. 'FACT {n}: {number} {unit}'
answer_types.list: array of short strings (technique names or kinds)
answer_types.timestamps: array of seconds from the start of the source
answer_types.rule: one procedural generation rule string, at most 400 characters, written in terms of parameters
answer_types.object: a JSON object with the keys the question's how_to_answer names

recipes.F3: Full-resolution crop (add ,scale=iw*2:-1:flags=lanczos to enlarge): ffmpeg -v error -ss T -i "$SRC" -frames:v 1 -vf "crop=W:H:X:Y" "$WORK/crop_T.png"
recipes.A1: Spectrogram image (add highpass=f=3000, before showspectrumpic to isolate clicks and whooshes): ffmpeg -v error -ss T -t D -i "$SRC" -lavfi "showspectrumpic=s=1200x600:legend=1" "$WORK/spec_T.png"

questions.question: What is the approximate reading grade of the narration (Flesch-Kincaid grade computed on the caption text)?
questions.why_it_matters: Fills script.reading_level so new scripts can be written at the same level.
questions.how_to_answer: Concatenate evidence.captions[].text in a scratch file (never into answers); compute FK grade = 0.39 x words/sentences + 11.8 x syllables/words - 15.59 with a simple vowel-group syllable count; delete the scratch file. Report word count in the note.
questions.challenge: Auto captions often lack punctuation, which inflates words per sentence; check sentence counting and lower confidence when punctuation is missing.

questions.question: What is the median number of words per sentence (or per caption-delimited phrase when punctuation is missing)?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets a sentence length budget for the script writer.
questions.how_to_answer: Split the caption text on sentence punctuation (or on caption card boundaries); report median and p90.
questions.challenge: State which split was used; card-based splits measure caption chunking, not sentences.

questions.question: Which point of view dominates the narration: first person, second person ('you'), third person, or mixed?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes the point_of_view parameter.
questions.how_to_answer: Count pronoun families (I/we, you/your, he/she/they/it) per 100 words in the caption text; report the dominant family and its share.
questions.challenge: 'You' in a quoted phrase or generic 'you' in third-person facts can mislead; check its use in context in two places.

questions.question: Which tense dominates: present, past, or mixed by section (for example past for history, present for explanation)?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes a tense rule for generated scripts.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify the main verb of each sentence; report shares per beat role.
questions.challenge: Sample five sentences and check the classification by hand.

questions.question: Which rhetorical devices appear, and how often (rhetorical question, rule of three, contrast 'not X but Y', superlative, imperative, analogy, cliffhanger, callback)?
questions.why_it_matters: Lists the devices the writer should reuse, with frequency.
questions.how_to_answer: Scan sentences for each device; record counts and the timestamps of each instance; never copy the sentence.
questions.challenge: Each device count needs at least one timestamp; spot-check two instances against the audio.

questions.question: What is the sentence template used inside an item (slots for subject, number, unit, consequence)?
questions.why_it_matters: Gives the per-item script pattern the generator fills.
questions.how_to_answer: Compare the first sentence of three items; keep the shared structure and replace content with typed slots, for example '{subject} {verb} {number} {unit}, {consequence}'.
questions.challenge: Test the template against a fourth item; if it does not fit, list the variants instead of forcing one.

questions.question: How many specific numbers (counts, dates, measurements, percentages) are stated per item, median?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes numbers_per_item and a constraint for content research.
questions.how_to_answer: Count digit groups and number words per item in captions; also check key-number overlays (F3 crops).
questions.challenge: Exclude label ordinals (FACT 2) and OCR noise; recount one item manually.

questions.question: Are claims attributed to sources in the narration or on screen ('according to', source captions, citations)?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets claims_need_sources and whether the format shows sources.
questions.how_to_answer: Search caption text for attribution phrases and scan F1 frames at item starts for small source text.
questions.challenge: Absence of attribution in the source does not mean variants may skip sources; note it, but the IR default stays true for factual formats.

questions.question: What share of sentences contain a concrete specific (number, named place, date, named object) rather than a general statement?
questions.why_it_matters: Captures specificity, which this project treats as a quality constraint.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify each sentence as specific or general; report the share. Do not copy sentences.
questions.challenge: Re-classify a random 20% sample; disagreement above 20% means low confidence.

questions.question: Does each item end with a consequence or 'so what' line that says why the fact matters?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes a per-item closing slot.
questions.how_to_answer: Inspect the last sentence of each item; mark whether it states an implication, outcome or comparison.
questions.challenge: Require the share of items with such a line; 'true' needs at least two thirds.

questions.question: What connective pattern links items (number callout, 'but', 'next', a question, no connective)?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes the transition phrase slot between items.
questions.how_to_answer: Look at the first two words of each item's first sentence and abstract them to a type, for example '{ordinal} callout' or 'contrast word'.
questions.challenge: If items start differently each time, answer 'no fixed connective' rather than inventing a pattern.

questions.question: Where does the script call back to the hook or an earlier item (timestamps)?
questions.why_it_matters: Adds a callback rule (for example payoff references the hook).
questions.how_to_answer: Find later sentences that repeat a key noun or number from the hook; list timestamps.
questions.challenge: A repeated topic word is not a callback unless it explicitly refers back.

questions.question: What register is the language in: casual or slang, neutral conversational, formal, or technical?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes the tone/register parameter.
questions.how_to_answer: Look at contractions, slang, jargon density and sentence complexity across the whole script.
questions.challenge: Register judged from the hook alone is over-generalised; check the middle and end.

questions.question: How many intensifiers or emphasis words (very, insane, literally, actually, huge) occur per minute of speech?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets an intensity budget; high values read as hype.
questions.how_to_answer: Count words from a fixed intensifier list in captions; divide by total speech minutes from audio.speech_segments.
questions.challenge: Report the word list used; counts depend on it.

questions.question: How many words does the whole narration contain, and how many words per second of runtime?
questions.why_it_matters: Gives the script length budget for a target duration.
questions.how_to_answer: Word count of captions; divide by source.duration_s.
questions.challenge: Check that captions cover the whole speech (compare caption span with speech_segments span).

questions.question: Is there a reversal or twist sentence, and at what fraction of the runtime?
questions.why_it_matters: Places a reversal beat in the format.
questions.how_to_answer: Find a sentence that contradicts an expectation set earlier (contrast word plus new information); give its start ratio.
questions.challenge: A contrast word alone is not a twist; the claim must invert something earlier.

questions.question: Does the script ask the viewer to predict or guess before a reveal?
questions.why_it_matters: Adds a predict-then-reveal pattern (a known learning technique) to the format.
questions.how_to_answer: Look for a question followed by a pause (speech_segments gap) and then an answer; list timestamps.
questions.challenge: Rhetorical questions answered immediately are not prediction prompts; require a gap of at least 0.5 s or an explicit prompt.

questions.question: How is jargon handled: defined inline, replaced by plain words, used without definition, or absent?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes a writing rule for technical topics.
questions.how_to_answer: Find technical terms in captions; check whether a definition clause follows within the same or next sentence.
questions.challenge: List how many terms were checked; one term is not enough for a rule.

questions.question: Do sentences put the key information first (number or claim up front) or build to it at the end?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes a sentence construction rule.
questions.how_to_answer: For sentences containing a number, note whether the number appears in the first or last third of the sentence.
questions.challenge: Report the counts behind the choice; a 55/45 split is 'mixed'.

questions.question: How many direct questions to the viewer does the script contain, and where?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets the question count and placement rule.
questions.how_to_answer: Count sentences ending in a question mark (or interrogative structure when punctuation is missing); list timestamps.
questions.challenge: Auto captions may drop question marks; check intonation on an A1 spectrogram for two instances.

questions.question: What does the closing line do: summarise, provoke a thought, ask a question, instruct (call to action), or tease another video?
questions.why_it_matters: Fills the outro line slot.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify the last sentence of the narration.
questions.challenge: Check that the 'last sentence' is not end-card boilerplate added after the content.

questions.question: Is there a recurring refrain or catchphrase structure (same phrase shape repeated across items)?
questions.why_it_matters: Adds a refrain slot that a new series fills with its own wording.
questions.how_to_answer: Look for repeated n-grams of 3+ words across items; describe only the shape (for example '{ordinal} reason: {claim}'), never the words.
questions.challenge: A repeated distinctive phrase belongs to the source; the pattern must not let it through.

questions.question: Does the on-screen text duplicate the narration word for word, summarise it, or add information the voice does not say?
questions.why_it_matters: Decides how caption and label text are generated from the script.
questions.how_to_answer: Compare F3 crops of on-screen text in three items with the caption text at the same time.
questions.challenge: If captions came from OCR, verbatim is circular; use the transcription adapter output or say not determinable.

questions.question: What emotional arc does the script follow (for example curiosity to surprise to satisfaction, fear to relief, problem to solution)?
questions.why_it_matters: Gives the writer an arc to follow; recorded as an observed pattern, not a judgement of quality.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify the dominant function of each beat (question, tension, reveal, resolution) and write the sequence.
questions.challenge: Emotional labels are interpretive; method must be 'inferred' and each step must cite a beat.

questions.question: Is the script a story (character, goal, obstacle, outcome) or a list of independent points?
questions.why_it_matters: Determines whether items can be reordered.
questions.how_to_answer: Check whether later items depend on earlier ones (references, continuity of a subject).
questions.challenge: Try mentally swapping items 2 and 3; if nothing breaks it is a list.

questions.question: How often are numbers made tangible with comparisons or analogies (for example 'as tall as {landmark}')?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets a comparison-per-item rule.
questions.how_to_answer: Count analogy or comparison constructions per item; report median.
questions.challenge: List the timestamps of counted instances.

questions.question: How much hedging language is used (may, might, some say, reportedly) per minute?
questions.why_it_matters: Indicates claim confidence style; informs fact-check strictness for variants.
questions.how_to_answer: Count hedge words per speech minute.
questions.challenge: Report the hedge list used.

questions.question: Are numbers spoken rounded ('about 3 million') or precise ('3,124,000')?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes a number formatting rule for scripts and overlays.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify each spoken number by significant figures; also check on-screen numbers.
questions.challenge: Years and ordinals are neither; exclude them from the count.

questions.question: What kinds of claims would a variant need to fact-check (statistics, dates, health, money, quotes, rankings)?
questions.why_it_matters: Tells the render pipeline which claim types require a cited source.
questions.how_to_answer: Classify each factual sentence by claim type; list the types present with counts.
questions.challenge: Health, money and safety claims must be listed if present at all, even once.

questions.question: What is the word budget for one item beat (median words per item and the words-per-second rate it implies)?
questions.why_it_matters: Becomes the generation rule words_per_item = item_beat_s x words_per_s.
questions.how_to_answer: Count caption words per item beat; divide by item beat duration.
questions.challenge: Recompute for two items; the rule must predict both within 20%.

questions.question: Which script properties should be parameters for a new topic (tone, point of view, words per item, numbers per item, sources shown)?
questions.why_it_matters: Feeds the parameteriser with typed script parameters.
questions.how_to_answer: Collect answers 003, 007, 013, 030 and propose parameters with defaults from the observed values and ranges from observed spread.
questions.challenge: Every proposed parameter must cite the question it comes from.

questions.question: Is there a sign-off or recurring closing formula?
questions.why_it_matters: Adds a closing slot that a new series fills with its own line.
questions.how_to_answer: Check the final 5 s of captions and the last text crop; describe the form only (for example '{series name} sign-off with handle').
questions.challenge: A sign-off containing the source's name or handle must not enter the format.

questions.question: How complex is the vocabulary for non-native listeners (share of words outside a common 3,000-word list, idiom count)?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets a plain-language constraint for localisable variants.
questions.how_to_answer: If a frequency list is available locally, compute the out-of-list share; otherwise count idioms and multi-syllable words per 100 words and mark the method inferred.
questions.challenge: If no word list was used, the answer must say so and confidence must be under 0.4.

questions.question: Does the narration address a specific audience group or situation ('if you are a {group}', 'when your {situation}')?
questions.why_it_matters: Adds an audience-address slot.
questions.how_to_answer: Search caption text for conditional address patterns; describe the shape only.
questions.challenge: Generic 'you' is not audience targeting; require an explicit group or situation.

questions.question: How many distinct claims or ideas does each sentence carry on average (one idea per sentence or packed sentences)?
questions.why_it_matters: Sets the density rule for script writing.
questions.how_to_answer: For 10 sentences, count independent clauses carrying new information; report the mean.
questions.challenge: Recount three of the sentences; disagreement means lower confidence.
